lines: A brazed tie-in is made only after the main is isolated and depressurised, and the oxygen level at the joint is confirmed at no more than 23%. Oil and grease are kept away from oxygen fittings.
A harness user never works alone. Anchors are rated for 12 kN with limited free fall or 15 kN with free fall, with enough clear distance to arrest a fall, and rescue procedures are set and practised.
A new outdoor power point and its circuit are installed by a licensed electrician with the circuit isolated and proved de-energised first, and are RCD protected.

A scaffold over 4 m is used only after written handover, and inspected at least every 30 days. Bricklaying and blocklaying need a heavy duty scaffold, rated up to 675 kg a bay, and bays are not overloaded.
A standby person stays outside, in continuous contact, and never enters to rescue. Rescue is started from outside.
A suitable fire extinguisher is kept at the work area while solvent-based primers or membranes are in use.
A temporary barrier is fixed across the gap before the old handrail is cut out, and stays until the new handrail is fixed.
A worker enters the trench to set a pit only where the trench is shored, benched or battered, and open pits are covered or fenced when no one is working at them.
An exclusion zone is fenced and signed around the structure, wide enough that falling or rebounding debris cannot reach anyone outside it. No one enters while demolition is under way.

An exclusion zone, sized by risk assessment and extended downwind, keeps out anyone not wearing RPE. Signs visible before entry say blasting is in progress, there is a dust hazard, access is for authorised persons only and RPE must be worn.
An exclusion zone, with signs and barricades, around trucks and plant while they load and unload.
An older meter panel is assumed to contain asbestos unless it has been tested, and no power tools are used on it.
Anchor holes are drilled with on-tool extraction, and a fit-tested respirator is worn.
Anchors and lines are fixed only to structure the designer or a competent person has confirmed can carry the load, to the manufacturer's instructions and AS/NZS 1891.4 and AS/NZS 5532.
Anchors drilled into concrete are drilled with on-tool extraction, and a fit-tested respirator is worn.
Any cutting of natural stone is done wet or with on-tool extraction, with a fit tested P2 respirator.

Any laser level or setting out laser is below class 3B (class 3B and class 4 lasers are banned in construction work), is used by a worker trained on it, and is set up so no one is exposed to the beam.
Any trench a worker enters has a ladder or safe ramp near the work, and a second way out at the other end of the open run so no one can be trapped by a slump.
Anyone still at risk of exposure after these controls is provided with, and wears, respiratory protective equipment that has been fit tested to them.
Anyone with an injection injury, even one that looks minor, goes straight to hospital for treatment.
Array conductors are energised in daylight and are treated as energised until isolated and proven de-energised: the DC isolator is opened first, and DC connectors are never pulled apart under load.
Asbestos likely to be disturbed is identified before demolition and, so far as is reasonably practicable, removed by a licensed asbestos removalist before demolition starts.

Assess in writing before starting whether the processing is high risk, including where the stone is only removed, repaired or modified. The assessment does not count PPE or administrative controls, and does not rely only on the dust controls used for the processing, such as wet methods, extraction or isolation.
Avoid lifting multiple loads at the same time (high/low loads), as it is difficult to ensure the dogger is not underneath them.
Bags and drums are moved by forklift, trolley or two people, and opened at waist height.
Bags are moved on trolleys or by the mixer delivery, and trowelling is rotated with other tasks.
Barricade open holes until the posts are set.
Barrow loads are kept small enough for one person to handle, and barrowing and screeding are rotated.
Battery caulking guns are used for long runs, and tasks are rotated.
Beams and rafters are lifted into place by two people or with a lifting aid.
Bearers and long timbers are carried by two people or moved on a trolley, and set down, not dropped.
Bearings are cut with a wet saw or with on-tool extraction, and the cutter wears a fit-tested respirator.

Before any work, a builder or engineer checks whether the wall carries the ceiling, roof or floor above. If it does, work stops: the temporary support and new beam are designed by an engineer and covered by their own SWMS.
Before demolition or refurbishment, a competent person identifies any asbestos in the structure, and it is removed so far as is reasonably practicable before the work starts.

Before directing a lift, the dogger checks each sling, shackle and lifting attachment has a working load limit at least equal to the load, the load is balanced, no part is loose, and it is not snagged.
Before entry to a deep or narrow pit, the air is checked. Where it could be poor, it is monitored while people are in the pit, and a person at the top keeps watch.

Before installed engineered stone is processed, written notice of the work, its type, and its frequency and duration is given to the regulator in the form it requires. Any change is notified within 30 days, work still going 12 months after the last notice is notified again within 30 days, and a copy of each notice is kept for 5 years.

Before removal, each service is located and disconnected at its source: electrical circuits by a licensed electrician, locked out and proved de-energised; water and drainage drained; gas purged by a licensed gas fitter.
Before termination at the main switchboard, the circuit is isolated, locked and proved de-energised, and live parts nearby are shrouded.

Before the work, a deep or enclosed pool shell is assessed against the confined space definition, because acid fumes collect at the bottom. If it is a confined space, the confined space steps and entry permit apply.

Before work on isolated plant or services, an isolation permit is issued by the principal contractor, or signed by the supervisor where the principal contractor does not issue them, listing each isolation point. Each point is locked and tagged by every worker on the job, and the plant or service is tested to prove it is dead, stopped or depressurised before work starts.
Benchtop cut-outs are cut with on-tool extraction, and natural stone benchtops are cut wet or with extraction, with a respirator worn.
Benchtops and heavy units are moved with trolleys or lifting aids, or by enough people for the weight.
Benchtops are carried by two people or more for their weight, and lifted onto the cabinets, not slid over the edge.
Bitumen is a combustible fuel: clear rubbish and other fuel from the area, and keep fire-fighting equipment at the work area.

Blasters also wear a protective suit closed at the wrists and ankles, canvas or leather gloves and protective footwear. The helmet cape is replaced immediately if damaged and never repaired with tape.
Blocks and fibre cement are cut with a wet saw or on-tool extraction, and a fit tested P2 respirator is worn.
Blocks are cut with a wet saw or a saw with on-tool extraction, never dry cut without extraction, and the cutter wears a fit tested P2 respirator.
Blocks are team lifted or moved by machine, and stacked close to the work.
Blocks or frames are lifted by two people or with lifting aids.
Boards are delivered close to the work, lifted to the level by crane or hoist, and moved on trolleys.
Boards are worked on at a comfortable height on stands or a tilting frame, and tasks are rotated.
Brazing is hot work under the site's hot work permit, with combustibles moved or covered and an extinguisher at hand.
Breaking concrete with power tools or plant is processing crystalline silica. Control it with wet suppression or on-tool extraction, and fit tested respirators for anyone still at risk.

Breaking masonry and slabs is processing a crystalline silica substance: water sprays keep dust down, and anyone still at risk wears a fit tested respirator. Hearing protection near breakers and hammers.
Breaking out and grinding concrete is processing a crystalline silica substance: use tools with on-tool extraction or water suppression, and wear a fit-tested respirator.

Bricks and blocks are not engineered stone, but cutting them with power tools is processing crystalline silica and must be controlled: wet cutting or on-tool extraction, and respirators for anyone still at risk.
Bricks and rubble are lowered in buckets or a chute to a closed-off area below, not thrown.
Brickwork is broken out with water to keep dust down, and a fit-tested respirator is worn.
Bulk bags and soil are landed and stored only where the slab is rated to take them, as the principal contractor directs.
Carpet tiles are moved in cartons on trolleys.
Carry cleaning gear in small loads, or move it with trolleys along the concourses.
Carry waste in small loads or use a chute or barrow to the skip, and rotate tasks.
Ceiling work is done from a platform ladder or mobile scaffold.
Cement and lime are bought in bags of 20 kg or less where the supplier offers them.
Chainsaw and mulcher noise is hazardous: anyone near them wears personal hearing protectors throughout the period of exposure, not just part of it.
Chase and drill with water or on-tool extraction. Anyone still at risk of exposure after these controls wears a fit tested respirator.
Chase and drill with water suppression or on-tool dust extraction. Anyone still at risk of exposure wears a fit tested respirator (P2 or better).
Circuits are isolated and proved de-energised before fittings are connected, and connections are made by licensed electricians.
Collect solvent and solvent-based paint waste in labelled containers and dispose of it promptly.
Combustion engines, generators and LPG forklifts are kept away from the openings, so exhaust gases such as carbon monoxide cannot build up in the space.
Compactor operators are rotated between tasks to limit hand-arm and whole-body vibration from vibrating compacting plates.
Components are lifted with two people or a lifting aid.
Consumer mains and submains are terminated at the new board only once each is proved de-energised at its source.
Containers of solvent-based paint and thinners are kept away from heaters and other heat sources, and lids are kept closed when not in use.
Conveyors, crushers and screens have guards fitted, and pull-wire and emergency stops are tested before each shift.
Cover or barricade every penetration as soon as it is formed. Covers withstand a fall onto them, are fixed in place so they cannot be moved by accident, and are marked as covering a hole.

Cover or barricade the hole as soon as it is cut. Covers are strong enough to take anyone who could fall onto them, securely fixed so they cannot be moved or removed by accident, and marked as covering a hole.

Cover or guard each bore as soon as it is formed. Covers are strong enough to take anyone who could fall onto them, securely fixed so they cannot be moved or removed by accident, and marked as covering a hole.
Crack surfaces are ground with on-tool extraction, and a respirator is worn.
Crane, hoist or barrow blocks to the work face, and stage them between waist and shoulder height. Training in lifting technique is not the main control.
Cut sections are lifted out with an excavator or bobcat, or broken into pieces small enough to lift by hand.

Cuts with an abrasive disc are hot work: they are made only under the site's hot work permit, with combustible materials cleared or covered, a fire extinguisher at the work, and a fire watch during the cutting and for at least 30 minutes after it stops.
Cutting concrete is processing a crystalline silica substance and must be controlled: wet cutting or on-tool extraction, and respirators for anyone still at risk.
Cutting concrete or asphalt is processing a crystalline silica substance, and existing asphalt and concrete are saw cut with water suppression or local exhaust ventilation (dust extraction).
Damper and collar fixings drilled into concrete or masonry are drilled with on-tool extraction, and a fit tested P2 respirator is worn.
Deliver and stack materials close to where they are used, and team lift long boards.
Disconnect the power before removing a guard, changing a blade or cutter, or clearing a jam, and refit the guard before use.
Disconnecting and reconnecting the power to an electric heater is electrical work for a licensed electrician, with the circuit isolated first.
Do not dig below the design stage level, or remove soil within the active soil zone, without a competent person's approval.
Do not over-reach: keep the centre of the torso within the ladder stiles, and face the ladder when going up, coming down or working from it.
Door panels are lifted into their frames or tracks with a door lifter or by two people, and held until they are fixed and adjusted.
Down conductors on the facade are installed from an EWP, swing stage or scaffold set out in the fall controls.
Drill anchors with on-tool dust extraction. Anyone still at risk of exposure wears a fit tested respirator (P2 or better).
Drill anchors with on-tool extraction. Anyone still at risk of exposure after this control wears a fit tested respirator.
Drill hanger anchors with on-tool extraction, and wear a fit tested P2 respirator.
Drill masonry and concrete for frame fixings with on-tool dust extraction. Anyone still at risk of exposure wears a fit tested respirator.
Drill with on-tool extraction. Anyone still at risk of exposure wears a fit tested respirator.

Drilling concrete for hanger anchors with a power tool is processing a crystalline silica substance and must be controlled: on-tool extraction or wet methods, and respirators for anyone still at risk. Assess in writing before drilling whether it is high risk, without counting PPE or administrative controls, and without relying only on the dust controls used for the processing. If it cannot be determined, treat it as a risk to health.
Drilling concrete is processing a crystalline silica substance. It is controlled by wet drilling, on-tool extraction or local exhaust.

Drilling concrete with a power tool is processing a crystalline silica substance and must be controlled: on-tool extraction or wet methods, and respirators for anyone still at risk. Assess in writing before drilling whether it is high risk, without counting PPE or administrative controls, and without relying only on the dust controls used for the processing. If it cannot be determined, treat it as high risk.
Drilling masonry, concrete or tiles is done with on-tool dust extraction, and a fit-tested respirator is worn where dust remains.

Drilling tiles and masonry with 1% or more crystalline silica with a power tool is processing that must be controlled: on-tool extraction or wet methods, and respirators for anyone still at risk. Assess in writing before drilling whether it is high risk, without counting PPE or administrative controls, and without relying only on the dust controls used for the processing. If it cannot be determined, treat it as a risk to health.
Duct access panels are opened from a platform ladder or mobile scaffold, and the roof fan is reached only with the roof edge protection or fall control set out for the roof.
During hot work, a fire extinguisher is kept at the work, and a fire watch checks the area, including below it, during the work and for at least 30 minutes after it stops.
Each pit is closed with a cover fixed in place and strong enough for anyone who could fall onto it, or with guard rails and toe boards, whenever no one is working in it.
Each worker fits a personal lock, and danger tags are removed only by the people who signed them.
Eaves are reached from a mobile scaffold, trestles with a platform, or a platform ladder, not from a ladder leaned on the gutter.
Edge finishing, which involves kneeling, is rotated with other tasks.

Edge protection and penetration covers stay in place. Covers are strong enough to take anyone who could fall onto them, securely fixed so they cannot be moved or removed by accident, and marked as covering a hole.
Edges of the empty pool shell are barricaded, and access into the shell is by a fixed ladder or stair.
Empty tanks are moved by enough people or with a lifting aid.
Equipment is visually inspected before it is tested, and damaged items are tagged out of service straight away.
Equipment that is due for testing but has not been tested is not used, for example by locking it away or fitting lock out labels and tags.
Every conductor is tested de-energised before the old board is touched. Anything that cannot be disconnected is treated as live and shrouded.

Every new floor opening is covered as soon as it is cut, with a cover strong enough to take anyone who could fall onto them, securely fixed so they cannot be moved or removed by accident, and marked as covering a hole. Wall openings at an edge have edge protection fixed before the section is removed.
Fire rated sealants and mastics for penetrations are used as their safety data sheets set out, with good ventilation and gloves resistant to the product.

Fit flashback arrestors at the torch and regulator. Keep cylinders upright and secured, valves closed when not in use, and turn the gas off at the valve straight after use. Gases heavier than air collect in pits and basements, so store and use cylinders where leaks can disperse.
Fixed work points in the sun, such as cutting and mixing stations, are shaded with a canopy, and fans or forced ventilation move air in enclosed hot areas.
Fixings into masonry or concrete are drilled with on-tool extraction, and a fit tested P2 respirator is worn.
Floor primers, adhesives and levelling compounds are used as their safety data sheets set out, with good ventilation and gloves, and the room stays closed to others until solvent vapour has cleared.
Flue pipes, cowls and liners on a building built before 2004 are treated as asbestos unless tested.
Footings and conduits for gates, booms and ticket machines are dug only after services are located.
Forklifts are kept apart from people, with a warning device. A forklift left unattended is parked level, with the brake on and the key removed.
Frames are raised with enough people or lifting equipment for their weight.
Frames are taken to upper floors by a materials hoist or other mechanical aid, not carried up ladders.
Framework that is not demolished is strong enough to remain safely in position, or is guyed or otherwise supported so it stays stable in adverse weather.
Gate leaves, posts, boom housings and arms are lifted with two people or a lifting aid.
Generators and tanks are lifted into place with a crane, with the load kept under control and within the crane's safe working limits.
Glass doors are hung with a door lifter or by two people on their pivots or hinges, and held until they are adjusted and their closers are set.
Gravel is moved with a bobcat or wheelbarrow, and shovelling is shared.
Grinding concrete is processing a crystalline silica substance and must be controlled: wet suppression, on-tool extraction or local exhaust, and respirators worn by anyone still at risk.
Grinding concrete is processing a crystalline silica substance, controlled by on-tool extraction or wet methods.
Grinding concrete is processing crystalline silica and must be controlled: wet suppression, on-tool extraction or local exhaust, and respirators for anyone still at risk.
Grinding steel is hot work: it is done only under the site's hot work permit, with a fire extinguisher at the work, and a fire watch during the grinding and for at least 30 minutes after it stops.
Grout around the cracked tiles is cut with an oscillating tool or grinder with on-tool extraction, and tiles are broken out with a chisel, with eye protection and a fit tested P2 respirator.
Growing media and materials are spread across the roof within the load limits the engineer sets, not stockpiled in one place.
Guards and emergency stops are fitted and tested before the plant is run, and it is isolated and locked out while anyone works on it.
Guards are fitted before the conveyor is run, and the drives are isolated and locked out whenever anyone works on the conveyor.
Guards taken off for the work are refitted and checked before the isolation is removed.
Guillotines, punches, press brakes and saws have their guards in place, strongly fixed and hard to bypass, with interlocks or presence-sensing devices where access is needed while they run.
Gutter and downpipe lengths are passed up to the platform by two people or lifted with a rope or hoist, not carried up a ladder.
Gutters are reached from an EWP, a scaffold or a roof with edge protection, not by leaning out from a ladder.
Hand signals, whistles, or bell and buzzer signals are agreed for use alongside radios or when radios are not available.
Hand-held breaking is eliminated by using plant-mounted breakers or other methods unless this is not reasonably practicable; otherwise use tools that produce less vibration.
Hangers are fixed from a mobile scaffold, EWP or platform ladder suited to the height, never from the top of a stepladder or from the grid.
Hard wiring, new power points and any change to the circuit are electrical work for a licensed electrician. Equipment is plugged into an RCD protected outlet.
Hardwired alarms are connected by a licensed electrician, with the circuit isolated and tested de-energised first.

Harness anchors are engineer designed or approved by a competent person, rated at least 12 kN for one person with a limited free fall, 15 kN for one person with a free fall, or 21 kN for two. Energy absorbers limit the arrest force to 6 kN, there is enough clearance below to stop a fall before it hits anything, and no one uses a harness system alone.
Harness anchors are rated at least 15 kN for one person with a free fall, there is enough clearance below, no one works alone on a harness, and the rescue plan is tested.
Hearing protection is worn the whole time workers are exposed to the noise. Workers who must wear it have hearing tests within 3 months and at least every 2 years.
Hearing protection is worn within the signposted area, and operators' exposure to vibration is managed by rotating tasks.
Hearing protection when breaking or grinding, and use of vibrating tools is rotated.
Heated bitumen and cutters are kept away from ignition sources, with an extinguisher on the sprayer.
Heaters are moved by two people or with a trolley.
Heavier than air vapour collects in low and enclosed areas, such as stairwells, pits and basements.
Heavy appliances are moved by two people or with a trolley.
Heavy beams and lintels are lifted with a hoist, block and tackle, gantry or other plant. Team lifts are planned, with the load shared and the route clear.
Heavy bollards, barriers and concrete stops are lifted with a team lift, a trolley or plant.
Heavy doors are moved on door trolleys and hung with a door lifter or by two people.
Heavy equipment is moved with trolleys, pallet jacks or skates, with enough people for a planned team move.
Heavy frames and units are moved with lifting equipment rated for them, not by hand.
Heavy items are lifted with a chain hoist or lifting device rated for the load, not by hand at height.
Heavy lids and grates are lifted with a lid lifter or plant, not by hand alone.
Heavy parts are lifted with a machine or by two people with lifting aids.
Heavy pots and root balls are moved on trolleys or lifted by two people, and plants are handled with gloves.
Heavy security doors are lifted by two people or with a door lifter.
Heavy valves and meters are lifted with two people or a lifting aid.
Heavy work and work in full protective clothing are scheduled for the early morning or the coolest part of the shift.
Helical bars and grout are fitted to the supplier's instructions, with gloves and eye protection when mixing the grout.
High glass is reached from a platform ladder or mobile scaffold.

High walls and ceilings over the stairs are reached from a stair platform or scaffold made for stairs, set level on the treads with guardrails, never from a ladder standing on the steps or a plank across the balustrade.
Holding sheets in place while fixing is a hazardous posture: prop or support sheets rather than holding them.
Holes are dug by a competent operator, with workers out of the plant's reach, and the holes are covered or fenced until they are poured.
Hose reels are lifted onto their brackets by two people or with a lifter.
Hose reels high on walls are fixed from a platform ladder or mobile scaffold.
Hot work permit, fire-resistant barriers, fire-fighting equipment at hand, cylinders secured, and flashback arrestors fitted.
Hydrant pipe lengths are lifted into place with a pipe lifter, hoist or chain block rated for their weight, not held up by hand while they are fixed.
Hydraulic hoses, couplings and lifters are inspected and maintained to the manufacturer's instructions, and stored hydraulic pressure is released before a hose is disconnected.
Hydraulic systems are inspected before the move and depressurised before any fitting is undone.

Identify the metals and coatings before welding, and keep fume below the exposure standard. Stainless steel fume contains chromium and nickel, and open arc welding, especially MIG and TIG, forms ozone.

If a duct or plenum is a confined space, it is entered only under a confined space entry permit, after a competent person's risk assessment recorded in writing, with signs at each entry, a standby person and connected plant isolated.
If the isolation cannot be confirmed, stop, treat the parts as live and keep out of the approach distance.
If work is incomplete at a change of shift, the last person replaces their danger tag or lock with an out-of-service or caution tag, and affected persons are told the work is not complete.
Impact wrenches and bolting are repetitive: rotate tasks.
In a boom EWP, the harness is attached to the EWP's anchor point. Booms of 11 m or more need a licensed operator. No one uses a fall arrest harness alone.
In a building built before 2004 (asbestos products were used until the national ban at the end of 2003), the flue, its lining and the heater are checked for asbestos before they are disturbed.

In a building built before 2004 (asbestos products were used until the national ban at the end of 2003), the old membrane, flashings and sealants are checked against the asbestos register or tested before they are disturbed.
In a building built before 2004 (asbestos products were used until the national ban at the end of 2003), the old tiles are checked against the asbestos register or tested before they are disturbed.
In a building built before 2004 (asbestos products were used until the national ban at the end of 2003), wall and ceiling linings are checked for asbestos before they are disturbed.
In a building built before 2004 (asbestos products were used until the national ban at the end of 2003), wall sheets and any sheeting under the tiles are checked for asbestos before they are broken.
In a house built before 2004 (asbestos products were used until the national ban at the end of 2003), the ceiling is checked for asbestos before it is drilled.
In hot weather, roof space work is planned for the cooler part of the day, with breaks and water.
Inspect the ladder before setting it up for broken rungs, stiles and footings. Faulty or damaged ladders are removed from service.

Installed engineered stone is cut, drilled or broken only to remove, repair, make minor modifications to or dispose of it, and only if the processing is controlled: the risks are minimised so far as is reasonably practicable, at least one of isolation from the dust, an enclosed operator cabin with high efficiency air filtration, wet dust suppression, on-tool extraction or local exhaust ventilation is used, and anyone still at risk wears respiratory protective equipment.
Jacks, pumps and hoses are rated for the loads, inspected before use, and the system is depressurised before any fitting is undone.
Joinery units and wall lining panels are designed and made in sections that a trolley, a lifter or two people can handle, with the largest piece agreed with the joinery shop before it is made.
Joints are cleaned out with a saw or grinder with on-tool extraction or water suppression, and a fit-tested respirator is worn.

Keep dust below the exposure standard, and monitor the air if unsure. Check each product's safety data sheet: a product with 1% or more crystalline silica is a crystalline silica substance, and power sanding or cutting it is processing that must be controlled, with a written assessment before it starts.
Keep dust below the exposure standard, and vacuum or wet clean instead of dry sweeping.
Keep noise below 85 dB(A) over 8 hours and 140 dB(C) peak, reducing it at the source first. Workers who must wear hearing protection have hearing tests within 3 months and at least every 2 years.

Keep noise below 85 dB(A) over 8 hours and 140 dB(C) peak. Hearing protection is worn the whole time workers are exposed to the noise. Workers who must wear it have hearing tests within 3 months and at least every 2 years.
Keep noise below 85 dB(A) over 8 hours and 140 dB(C) peak. Hearing protection worn for the whole time of the noise, with hearing tests within 3 months of starting and at least every 2 years.

Keep noise below 85 dB(A) over 8 hours and 140 dB(C) peak. If you need to raise your voice to talk to someone 1 m away, the noise is likely hazardous. Change the way work is done so less noise is produced.

Keep noise below 85 dB(A) over 8 hours and 140 dB(C) peak. If you need to raise your voice to talk to someone 1 m away, the noise is likely to be hazardous. Hearing protection is worn the whole time workers are exposed to the noise, in signposted areas, with hearing tests within 3 months of starting and at least every 2 years.
Keep vapour below the exposure standard. Vapour heavier than air collects low down: extract from the lowest point and bring fresh air in from above.
Kneeling is a hazardous posture: rotate tasks and take short frequent breaks.
Kneeling to lay floor coverings is a hazardous posture: rotate tasks and take short frequent breaks. Replace hand tools with power tools to reduce force.
Kneeling while laying tiles is a hazardous manual task. Rotate tasks and take short, frequent breaks.
Kneeling while trowelling concrete is an awkward posture: use long-handled floats and edgers, and kneel only for edges and corners they cannot reach, to limit time kneeling.
Ladders are not set up on a scaffold platform, balcony or roof to gain extra height, or over a void.
Landing gates are fitted at each new level.
Large frames are lifted with a panel lifter or two people, with one person in charge.
Lead is an ototoxic substance: noise exposure of workers cutting or grinding lead is reduced to 80 dB(A) or below, and they undergo audiometric testing.
Lids stay on except when pouring, and spills are contained and cleaned up straight away.
Long boards and sheets are moved with a trolley or by a planned two-person lift, and delivered close to where they are used.
Long gutters and slot drains are carried by two people or on a trolley.
Long lengths are carried by two people.
Long periods kneeling are a hazardous manual task: rotate tasks.
Loose and leaning sections are taken down from the top, or propped, before anyone works below them.
Low odour, solvent-free sealants are used where the specification allows.
Machine controls are marked, guarded against starting by accident, and can be locked off. Emergency stops are red and within reach of each operator.
Manual handling: move props, frames, beams and ply to the work area in crane-lifted bundles, on trolleys or by hoist, not by carrying them across the floor.
Manual handling: no manual lifting of heavy boards; use skates, jacks and team handling for final positioning.
Manual handling: team lift long or heavy items, keep loads close to the body, and limit lifting above shoulder height.
Manual handling: team pull, rotate tasks, and keep cable bends and pulling points within reach without twisting.
Mark hot pipe as hot. Wear fire-resistant gloves, natural fibre clothing and filter eye protection for the flame.
Material boxes are engineer designed and certified, marked with their tare mass and SWL, lifted on four chains, with loads secured and not stacked above the sides.

Material that may be asbestos is either assumed to be asbestos or sampled by a competent person and analysed by a NATA-accredited laboratory, or one approved or operated by the regulator. Samples are sealed and double bagged.
Modules are lifted with a lifting aid or a planned team lift, within the manufacturer's weights.
Move boards on skates, trolleys or jacks.
Move racks and batteries with trolleys, pallet jacks or lifting aids. Team lifts are an interim control, with one person in charge.
Neighbouring buildings are protected before digging, and the work does not flood them.
No combustion engine plant in a trench or pit while workers are in it. Check the atmosphere before starting.

No hot work (welding, brazing, soldering or thermal cutting) starts until a hot work permit is issued by the principal contractor, or signed by the supervisor where the principal contractor does not issue them. The permit records the area cleared of combustible material, the fire extinguisher at the work and the fire watch, who checks the area for at least 30 minutes after the hot work stops.
No one climbs the tower alone, and the rescue equipment is kept at the tower so a rescue can start at once.
No one enters the pit until it has been assessed. A pit that is a confined space is entered only under the confined space steps: permit, atmosphere testing, standby person and rescue plan.
No one enters the tank, arrestor or pit. Work is done from outside, with the lid open only while needed and the opening guarded.
No one enters the wet well once it is placed. It is a confined space, and any entry is made only under a confined space entry permit, with the atmosphere tested and a standby person at the top.
No one enters the wet well, and work at the well is done from outside it.
No one stands between the item and the extraction airflow, and items hang far enough inside the booth to avoid rebound.
No one stands or walks on the polycarbonate sheets. Sheets are changed from a platform ladder or mobile scaffold beside or under the pergola.
No one uses the stair until the handrails and balustrade are fixed.

No person enters a confined space until a confined space entry permit is issued by the competent person named for the entry, after the air in the space is tested, with a standby person outside the space for the whole entry.
No watches, jewellery or other metal personal items. Fire extinguishers suitable for electrical fires are at hand.
Old fibro sheets on a shed built before 2004 are treated as asbestos unless tested, and are removed under the asbestos rules.
Old lead flashing is handled with gloves and hands are washed before eating. It is not burnt or ground.
Old mortar is broken out by hand, wet, and tiles are cut with a wet saw or a saw with on-tool extraction, with a P2 respirator worn.
Old posts are pulled with a post puller, jack or machine, not by hand, as a post that suddenly comes free applies a sudden force to the back.
Old roof sheets on a building built before 2004 (asbestos products were used until the national ban at the end of 2003) are checked for asbestos cement before they are disturbed.
Old stairs are taken apart from the top down, with the stringers propped until they are released, and are not pulled down in one piece.

On a building built before 2004 (asbestos products were used until the national ban at the end of 2003), fibre cement eaves linings, gutters and downpipes are treated as asbestos unless tested, and are not cut, drilled or broken until they have been.
On suspended floors, rubble is not left to build up beyond what the floor can carry (wet rubble weighs more), and buffers stop plant going over edges or into openings where it pushes debris.
Once uncovered, the open tank is barricaded and covered when no one is at it.
Open bores are covered or barricaded until they are concreted.
Open holes are covered or barricaded when no one is at them.
Open pits are barricaded and covered when no one is at them.
Open set-downs and recesses are covered or barricaded so no one can fall into them.
Openings in the deck are barricaded or covered as soon as boards are removed.
Openings in the deck are made safe as soon as they are formed, with covers or barricading.
Order smaller bags, or have bulk loads moved by machine. Deliver as close as possible to where the materials are used. Use mechanical aids, and rotate tasks.
Order the smaller or lighter bag and box sizes the supplier offers, have materials delivered as close to the room as possible, and use a trolley.
Order the smaller or lighter bag and box sizes the supplier offers, have materials delivered as close to the work area as possible, move them between levels by hoist or crane, and use trolleys.
Overhead work is broken up with other tasks, and tiles are cut on a bench with a knife or a saw with dust extraction.

Panel saws, table saws, docking saws, routers, spindle moulders, planers and CNC machines have their guards in place, strongly fixed and hard to bypass, with interlocks or presence-sensing devices where access is needed while they run.
Panels and bases are carried by two people or moved on a trolley.
Panels and tracks are carried by two people.
Panels are carried by two people and clamped as soon as each is placed, and are not handled in strong wind.
Panels are carried by two people where they are large.
Panels are lifted with a panel lifter or by two people.
Panels are lifted with a vacuum lifter or two people.

Pavers are not engineered stone, but cutting pavers with 1% or more crystalline silica is processing that must be controlled: wet cutting or on-tool extraction, and respirators for anyone still at risk. Assess in writing before cutting whether it is high risk, without counting PPE or administrative controls, and without relying only on the dust controls used for the processing. If it cannot be determined, treat it as a risk to health.
Pendants are lifted with a material lifter or lifting frame rated for the load, never held overhead by hand.
Penetrations keep their covers until they are sealed. Mesh over a penetration also has a solid cover over it.
Pipe is moved with mechanical aids or by two people.
Pipe is tied or clipped to the mesh at the spacing in the heating design, with tying tools to limit bending, and kneeling tasks are rotated with knee pads worn.
Pipes are cleaned and inspected with jetters and cameras from the surface. No one enters an access chamber unless it has been assessed and a confined space permit is in place.
Plant does not collide with people, and has a warning device where it could.
Plant is parked on level ground, the engine stopped, the key removed, and the plant isolated and tagged before work starts. Wheels are chocked.
Plant left unattended is parked on a firm, level surface with parts that lower under gravity lowered, the handbrake applied, the motor off and the key removed.
Plant with a combustion engine, such as a compressor or generator, is never used in the trench while workers are in it. Where engine exhaust could collect, ventilate and monitor for carbon monoxide.
Plants are moved across the roof in crates or on trolleys, and heavy pots and root balls are lifted by two people.
Platforms for erecting formwork are at least 450 mm wide, such as two scaffold planks. No one works from a single plank or bearer, or climbs the framework.
Ply sheets are carried by two people or with sheet lifters, and sheet handling stops when wind lifts the sheets.
Pod bundles and vapour barrier rolls are moved on trolleys.
Power to the wet walls and ceiling is isolated and locked out, and the wiring and fittings are checked by a licensed electrician before work starts.
Primers and membranes are used as their safety data sheets set out. In a narrow excavation, fumes are ventilated and no ignition sources are used near solvents.
Primers and sealants are used as their safety data sheets set out, with gloves, eye protection and ventilation, and away from ignition sources.
Pumps, filters and vessels are moved with skates, a pallet jack or lifting aids.
Put solvent-soaked rags in a closed metal container or take them off site.
Racks are carried by two people, and footings are dug only after services are located.
Rail sections, the chair and the motor are carried by two people.
Rails welded on site are hot work: a fire extinguisher is at hand, dry grass is cleared or wetted, and the welder wears a welding helmet, gloves and natural fibre clothing.
Raised buckets, blades and bodies are lowered, or blocked with their mechanical locks, before anyone works under them.
Raking out mortar joints for the flashing is done with on-tool extraction and a P2 respirator.
Raking out mortar with a power tool is processing a crystalline silica substance: use a tool with on-tool extraction, or hand tools, and wear a fit-tested respirator.
Reglets are cut into concrete with a saw fitted with water suppression or on-tool extraction, and the written silica assessment covers the reglet cutting.
Release pressure and isolate before clearing a blockage. Refit guards before restarting.
Remove supports in reverse order of installation, installing temporary members first wherever the engineer's removal sequence shows them, with workers kept clear.
Removing tiles and render with power tools is processing a crystalline silica substance: use wet methods or on-tool extraction, with respirators for anyone still at risk.
Render is mixed with a mixer or paddle, and bags are moved with a trolley.

Repeated drilling and fixing is a hazardous manual task (repetition, awkward posture and vibration from drills): rotate tasks, use drill stands for repeated holes, and have seats delivered by truck or crane to the tier where they are fitted.
Repetitive fixing is broken up with other tasks.
Respirators stay on until coveralls are vacuumed or removed inside out and bagged, and personal washing, including hands and fingernails, is done.
Riser covers and screens stay in place, and any opened section is fenced while it is open.

Risers and shafts are covered or screened at each level. Covers are strong enough to take anyone who could fall onto them, securely fixed so they cannot be moved or removed by accident, and marked as covering a hole.
Rock drilling noise is hazardous: the area around the rig is sign-posted as a hearing protector area, and no one enters it without personal hearing protectors, however short the stay.
Rollers keep back from soft edges, table drains and batters, and the operator wears the seatbelt.
Rolls are delivered close to the work, moved between levels by hoist or lift, and moved on trolleys.

Roof cavities get very hot: in hot weather, roof space work is done in the morning, in spells of no more than 30 minutes with a break outside the roof space between them, and workers take drinking water in with them.
Roof edge protection is in place before work starts near the edge, and no one works outside it without travel restraint to the roof anchors.
Roof sheets and walls are fixed from an elevating work platform or platform ladder, not by climbing the frame.
Rotate tying tasks, and use a tying tool or long-handled tier to limit bending.

Rubber softfall binders are used as their safety data sheet sets out, with gloves, eye protection and good ventilation. Workers using isocyanate binders have the respiratory protection and health monitoring the data sheet calls for.
Saw and grinder guards are in place and hard to bypass. Isolate the cutting area, wear a face shield, and replace worn blades and wheels.
Saws, shears, guillotines and press brakes have their guards in place, strongly fixed and hard to bypass, with interlocks or presence-sensing devices where access is needed while they run.
Screed is moved by barrow or pump, not carried in buckets. Screeding while kneeling is rotated with other tasks.
Screen panels are moved with a crane, hoist or trolley, not carried to the edge by hand.

Sealants and primers are applied as their safety data sheets set out, with chemical resistant gloves and eye protection, and the respirator the data sheet lists where vapour or spray can be breathed in.
Seats are handled by two people or with trolleys, and stacked close to where they are fixed.
Sections are cut to a size that plant or two people can handle, supported or slung before the last cut, and lowered under control, never dropped.
Services are located before footings are bored or excavated, and open holes are covered.
Services in the ceilings and partitions are isolated and made safe by the licensed trades before strip-out.
Services to the attached structure are disconnected and capped by the licensed trades, and the shared wall is propped or protected.
Shaft openings are barricaded at every level except while the door at that level is being fitted.

Shaft openings have barriers or fixed covers as soon as they are formed: covers are strong enough to take anyone who could fall onto them, securely fixed so they cannot be moved or removed by accident, and marked as covering a hole. Edge protection top rail at least 900 mm.
Shielding panels are moved on trolleys and lifted with panel lifters or two people, and propped until fixed.
Signs and screens are lifted with a crane, hoist or EWP rated for the load, not carried up ladders.
Signs are lifted with a crane, hoist or EWP rated for the load, not carried up ladders.
Sleepers and posts are team lifted or moved by machine.
Sleepers and rail are handled with on-track plant or sleeper tongs, never lifted by hand alone.
Sleepers and steel panels are carried by two people, and stacked close to where they are used.
Sloping and wet surfaces are a fall hazard: wear slip resistant footwear.
Sludge and debris are removed with a vacuum truck from the surface wherever possible, so the time anyone spends in the well is kept short.
Smaller bags are used where the product comes in them, and bags are stacked near the mixer or barrow, in front of the worker and between waist and shoulder height.
Smaller rock placed by hand is limited to pieces one person can handle.
Smoke and fire dampers are lifted into place with a hoist, lifter or two people.
Soldering or brazing is done under a hot work permit with ventilation.
Speed humps are lifted into place by two people or with plant.
Spent abrasive and dust are collected by vacuum recovery or wet methods, never by sweeping or compressed air blowdown, and waste is covered so it cannot become airborne.
Spoil is lifted out of deep pits with hoisting equipment kept in good order.

Spraying makes a hazardous airborne concentration likely. Ventilate, and wear the respirator the safety data sheet lists, even with other controls in place. Two-pack isocyanate paints: full-face air-fed respirators.
Steel or timber frame members are supported before they are cut so they cannot spring, twist or drop, and are lowered under control with tag lines.

Stone is cut with a wet saw or a saw with on-tool extraction, or split by hand, never dry cut without extraction, and the cutter wears a fit tested P2 respirator. Cutting stone with a power tool is processing a crystalline silica substance.
Stone is split or cut wet or with on-tool extraction, with a fit tested P2 respirator and eye protection.
Stone, tiles and blocks are cut wet or with on-tool extraction, and the cutter wears a fit-tested respirator.
Stop handling sheets in strong wind.
Stringers and treads are carried by two people.
Stud holes are drilled with on-tool extraction, and a fit-tested respirator is worn.
Stud welding is done with screens, eye and face protection rated for welding, and ventilation. Cables and the stud welder are checked before use.
Sun protection: hat, long sleeves, sunglasses and SPF 30 or higher sunscreen. Drinking water, shade and rest breaks in hot weather.
Tasks are rotated to limit time kneeling.

Team carrying on stairs puts most of the weight on the handler at the lower end: move rail sections, chair and motor with a hoist or powered stair-climbing hand truck, and carry by hand only parts these cannot take.
Team lifts are an interim control only, with one person in charge. Training in lifting technique is not the main control.
Temporary cables are kept off access routes, materials are stacked away from fences and hoardings, and emergency exits stay clear and lit.
Testing that requires dismantling the electrical equipment is carried out only by a licensed electrical worker.
The BMU is used only by workers trained in its operation, to the building's BMU operating manual, after the daily pre-use check.
The area below and beside the wall is fenced off while the wall is unstable.
The boiler is moved on skates or a pallet jack, or lifted with a crane or forklift rated for its weight.

The bridge is taken down in the sequence the engineer's demolition plan sets, with spans propped or supported as it requires, and kept stable at every stage. No one works on or under a span while it is cut, broken or lifted out.
The ceiling or roof load is propped each side of the damaged section before any stud, plate or lintel is cut out, and the props stay until the new members are fixed.
The chimney is taken down by hand from the top, one course at a time, working from a scaffold or platform around it, never by pulling it over.
The circuit is isolated at the switchboard, locked and tagged, and proved de-energised before the old appliance is disconnected.
The consumer mains are tested de-energised before work starts, and the board is treated as live until they are.
The conveyor is commissioned to a written procedure, with emergency stops and pull wires tested first.
The crane is assembled and dismantled to the manufacturer's procedure by its trained erection crew, on firm, level ground checked for the loads.
The crane is inspected and its safety devices tested before its first lift.
The current safety data sheet for each pre-treatment chemical is at the work area, and every container, including anything decanted, is labelled.

The current safety data sheet is at the work area, the product is on the register, and containers are labelled. Use water-based paint instead of solvent-based paint, unless the paint specification calls for a solvent-based product.
The current safety data sheet is at the work area. Use mechanical fixing or the least hazardous sealant the glazing specification allows, and gloves resistant to the product.
The dock is closed to trucks and forklifts, and the open dock edge is barricaded until the leveller is fixed.
The door is lifted into place by two people or with a lifter, and held until its brackets are fixed.
The doorway or landing at the top of the stairs is barricaded while the stairs are out, and no one uses them until the new stairs and handrails are fixed.
The excavation is battered, benched or shored as the geotechnical advice or excavation plan sets out, and its edges are barricaded.
The fan and hood lighting are connected by a licensed electrician.
The floor is broken for drainage and the walls broken down with an excavator working from outside the pool, with no one in the pool while the plant works.
The gas detector stays on in the well while sludge is disturbed, and everyone leaves at once if it alarms.
The heater is moved with a trolley or by two people.
The kerb machine has its guards in place, and no one is near the auger or mould while it runs.
The letterbox bank is moved on a trolley, with a crane truck or by enough people for its weight, and propped or held until it is fixed.
The light head, solar panel and battery are fitted to the pole on the ground where the manufacturer allows, so less work is done at height.
The low voltage side of the transformer, including any construction supply or generator that could back-feed it, is isolated and locked off by a licensed electrician before work starts.
The masonry above is propped or needled before the old lintel is cut out, so the structure stays stable.
The mixer is guarded and stopped before anyone reaches into it.
The old appliance is moved out by two people or on a trolley.
The old awning is supported by the crane, forklift or props before its fixings or tie rods are released, and lowered, never let fall.
The old inverter is isolated on both its AC and DC sides, and the DC isolators locked off, before it is disconnected and removed.
The old membrane is lowered in a chute or a hoist, never thrown.
The old wall tiles are chipped off with a bolster or an oscillating tool, using on-tool extraction to keep dust down, with eye protection and a fit tested P2 respirator.
The open edge left as the screen moves is closed off or protected by edge protection until the screen is back in place.
The open edges and stair openings are protected with temporary rails until the permanent balustrade is fixed.
The open pit is guarded until the new lid is seated.
The opening in the roof is covered or sheeted over before work stops for the day.

The opening is covered as soon as it is cut, with a cover strong enough to take anyone who could fall onto it, securely fixed so it cannot be moved or removed by accident, and marked as covering a hole.
The opening is covered or barricaded as soon as it is cut, until the duct or upstand is in place.
The permanent balustrade and stair are fitted before the floor is used.

The pit is assessed. If it is a confined space: a written entry permit from a competent person, the atmosphere tested before entry, continuous communication, a standby person at the pit, and practised first aid and rescue procedures.
The plant's pumps, blower and alarm are wired and connected by a licensed electrician.
The pool light circuit is isolated and locked out at the switchboard and tested de-energised before the light or its cable is touched.
The pool's power and plumbing are disconnected and capped or made safe before work starts.
The pump is plugged into an existing RCD-protected outlet, or its supply is installed by a licensed electrician.
The regulator is notified before an underground tank of flammable liquid is abandoned, and placards and signs are removed once it no longer holds hazardous chemicals.
The roof is propped each side of the section before a post, beam or rafter is cut out, and the props stay until the new members are fixed.
The rotating rods are guarded, and no one handles rods while they turn. The rig has a working emergency stop.
The saw wheel or chain has its guards in place, and no one is within reach of it while it turns.
The site is secured from unauthorised access, and the edge near the street is supported against traffic loads.
The spa is moved with trolleys, a crane or enough people for its weight, on a planned route.
The stair opening is covered or has a guardrail at all times until the stair and its balustrade are fixed.
The test supply is from an RCD protected outlet or a dedicated test panel with its own isolator, and is isolated, locked and tagged before covers are removed or wiring is changed.
The transformer is set down in a bunded tray, with a spill kit suitable for PCB oil at hand so any spillage is contained and cleaned up.
The trencher's guards stay in place, and the engine is stopped and the plant isolated before anything is cleared from it.
The unit is lifted with a material lifter rated for its weight, never held overhead by hand, and is fixed to its hangers or supports before the lifter is lowered.
The unit is lowered and lifted with a material lifter rated for its weight, never held overhead by hand.
The unit is moved by two people or with a trolley.
The well is not entered. Working from the top, the pump is lifted with a davit or tripod and its lifting chain, up its guide rails.
Tiles and stone tops are drilled with on-tool extraction or water, and a respirator is worn.

Tiles and stone with 1% or more crystalline silica are a crystalline silica substance. Cutting them with power tools is processing that must be controlled: wet cutting or on-tool extraction, never dry cutting, and respirators for anyone still at risk.
Tiles are changed from a platform ladder or mobile scaffold suited to the height, never from the top of a stepladder, a desk or the grid.
Tiles are cut with a wet saw or a saw with on-tool extraction, and a fit-tested respirator is worn.
Tiles are cut with a wet saw or a saw with on-tool extraction, never dry cut without extraction.
Tiles, the bath hob and screed are broken out with water or on-tool extraction, with a fit tested P2 respirator worn, and the dust is cleaned up with an H class vacuum.
Tiling walls means long periods of reaching: work at a height between the hips and shoulders where the access allows it, rotate tasks, and take short, frequent breaks.
Tip guard and trigger lock are fitted and working, pressure is released before cleaning, and any injection injury gets immediate medical treatment, even if it looks minor.
Tippers tip clear of overhead power lines, and are kept from colliding with workers on foot.
To reduce whole-body vibration, operators adjust their suspension seats appropriately and operate plant within the speed suggested by the manufacturer or at a speed that reduces vibration levels.
Toe boards on edge protection, and exclusion zones and no go areas below.
Toilets are provided at no less than 1 pan per 15 males (and 1 urinal per 20 males) and 1 pan per 10 females, with a means to dispose of sanitary items, and are kept clean and not used for storage.
Top courses of wall tiles are reached from a platform ladder or step platform, not a stepladder, a bucket or the edge of a bath or bench.
Torch-on membrane is laid under a hot work permit, with an extinguisher at hand and gas cylinders kept upright at the top of the excavation, not in it.
Torch-on work is hot work under the site's hot work permit, with an extinguisher at hand, and gas cylinders kept upright and away from the flame.

Tower climbing is done only by workers trained in tower climbing and rescue, attached at all times to the tower's fall arrest system or with twin lanyards, with a rescue plan and rescue kit on site for a worker suspended in a harness.

Travel restraint may not be practicable on fragile roofing or slopes over 15 degrees, where fall arrest may be more appropriate. Where fall arrest is used near edges, swing down is controlled with guard rails or mobile anchors.
Treat every exposed part as energised until it is isolated and tested by a competent person and found de-energised.

Trench shields protect workers if a collapse happens, but do not support the ground: they are not loaded beyond their design, and are used to the manufacturer's instructions. Enter sheeted areas only by ladder.
Trenches and pits are secured from unauthorised or accidental entry. Lift pits have a lockable cover or a guard rail with a gate.

Trestle platforms where a person could fall 2 m or more (3 m in housing construction) have their trestles secured, edge protection, and a platform at least 450 mm wide and no higher than 5 m. Where a person could fall less than that (2 m, or 3 m in housing construction), the platform is at least 450 mm wide (225 mm for light work). Use only purpose-made pins.
Turf rolls are moved with the bobcat or by two people.
Two people carry long bearers and joists, or use mechanical aids. Rotate kneeling work.
Units are moved and placed by crane, not by hand. Bearing pads and fixings are handled in small loads, with tasks rotated.
Units go to upper floors by the goods lift, a hoist or a crane, not carried up stairs or ladders.
Use RCD protected tools and leads, and keep leads off wet floors and out of access ways.
Use a post hole digger or auger.
Use a turf laying machine for large turf rolls. Use mechanical aids for smaller rolls, and rotate tasks.
Use a tying tool or long-handled tier so fixers do not bend the back forward for long periods while tying.
Use barrows and trolleys for posts, sheets and concrete bags, order the smaller bag sizes the supplier offers, and rotate tasks.
Use barrows and trolleys for posts, wire rolls and concrete bags, order the smaller bag sizes the supplier offers, and rotate tasks.
Use door lifters, wedges and props to hold doors while they are hung, rather than holding them up by hand for long periods.
Use extension poles for walls and ceilings, with a platform used only for areas a pole cannot reach.
Use handling aids for pavers. Kneeling is a hazardous posture.
Use lifting aids, straps, trolleys and props to hold units while fixing, rather than holding them up by hand for long periods.
Use long-handled tools, rotate tasks and take breaks.
Use pipe lifters or jacks to hold pipe overhead, rather than holding it up by hand.
Use sheet lifters and suction pads or hooks, with training in each aid. Have sheets delivered to the floor where they are used.
Use water suppression or on-tool dust extraction when cutting or breaking masonry or concrete.
Vacuum or wet clean dust, never dry sweep.
Vacuum truck engines and other combustion engines are kept away from the opening so exhaust gases do not contaminate the air in the well.
Vanities, toilets and basins are moved by two people or on a trolley.
Ventilate as the label says: natural ventilation suits only small amounts of low toxicity products. Use fans or extraction otherwise.

Ventilate or purge, never with oxygen or any gas mixture with more than 21% oxygen. Test from outside for oxygen (19.5% to 23%), flammable gas (below 5% of the lower explosive limit) and toxic gases such as hydrogen sulphide and carbon monoxide.
Wall and ceiling panels are moved with panel trolleys and lifted with panel lifters or two people, and wall panels are propped until joined.
Wall sheets and screeds under old tiles are checked for asbestos first in a building built before 2004.
Waste is moved in wheelie bins, barrows or trolleys rather than carried, and bins and bags are not filled beyond what one person can move.
Wear filter eye protection rated for gas cutting, fire-resistant gloves and natural fibre clothing.
Wear gloves resistant to the product used, and no eating, drinking or smoking in the work area.

Welders wear eye, face and head protection with the right filter, fire resistant gloves covering hands and wrists, natural fibre clothing without pockets or folds that catch sparks, and footwear that will not trap sparks in laces or openings.
Welding is done in a welding bay with local exhaust ventilation at the arc, and respiratory protection where fume is not controlled.
When generators are run for testing, the exhaust is taken outside and the room ventilated so no one breathes diesel exhaust above the exposure standard.

Where a crane holds a section while it is cut free, the section's weight is worked out first (by cutting and weighing samples where the drawings do not give it), and the crane's rated capacity is at least 1.5 times that weight.
Where a diesel pump is run indoors, the pump room is ventilated and the exhaust is taken outside, so no one breathes diesel exhaust above the exposure standard.
Where a person could fall from a cut face or batter crest, install barriers or bunds, and set up clear pedestrian detours.
Where an opening is vertical, it is protected so people cannot fall in.
Where anchors are drilled repetitively into the soffit, the drill is supported on a drill stand or overhead drilling rig so it is not held with the hands above shoulder height.
Where concrete is ground or patched, it is done with on-tool extraction or wet methods, and a fit tested P2 respirator is worn where dust remains.
Where concrete or paving is cut to reinstate it, it is cut wet or with on-tool extraction, anyone still at risk wears a fit tested P2 respirator, and the written silica assessment covers the cutting.

Where control joints are saw cut, or concrete is cut or drilled, it is done wet or with on-tool extraction. This is processing a crystalline silica substance. Anyone still at risk of exposure wears a fit tested P2 respirator.
Where edge protection must be opened to build at the edge, access to the open edge is by permit only, with a travel restraint system.

Where fall arrest is used instead of restraint: harness anchors are engineer designed or approved by a competent person, rated at least 12 kN for one person with a limited free fall, 15 kN for one person with a free fall, or 21 kN for two. Energy absorbers limit the arrest force to 6 kN, there is enough clearance below to stop a fall before it hits anything, and no one uses a harness system alone.
Where fall arrest is used instead, anchors are engineer designed or approved by a competent person, no one works alone, and the rescue procedure is tested.

Where fall arrest is used, anchors are tested and approved by a competent person before first use and meet the anchor strength in AS/NZS 1891.4, there is enough clearance below that the user cannot hit the ground or another surface, no one uses it alone, at least one other person on site can rescue them, and the rescue procedure is tested.

Where gas or contaminated soil is known or suspected in the excavation, airborne contaminants are managed: a gas monitor is worn by anyone in it, and mechanical ventilation is used whenever the monitor alarms or the material is known to give off vapour or gas.
Where hand-held breakers are used, operators are rotated to limit time on the tool, and the lightest breaker that does the job is used to cut vibration.

Where other boilers or hot plant in the room stay in operation, the area has artificial extremes of temperature, which makes the work high risk construction work: plan breaks, cool water and limits on time near hot plant.

Where posts are set in paving or concrete, core or cut the hole with water suppression or on-tool extraction, as cutting concrete and pavers releases silica dust. Anyone still at risk of exposure wears a fit tested P2 respirator.
Where soffits and walls are patched after stripping, it is done from a mobile scaffold with its castors locked, or a platform ladder, not from a stepladder.

Where temporary edge protection must be opened, access to the opening is under a permit system. Workers at the opening use travel restraint so they cannot reach the edge. No one uses a fall arrest harness while working alone.

Where the space is hot, time inside is limited to set periods written on the entry permit, forced ventilation brings in cooler air, and entrants rest and drink water outside the space between periods.
Where the walls could slump onto a worker, such as in sandy, wet, fissured or previously dug ground, the trench is shored, benched or battered before entry, even when it is shallower than 1.5 m.

While the old skylight is out, the opening is covered with a cover strong enough to take anyone who could fall onto it, securely fixed so it cannot be moved or removed by accident, and marked as covering a hole.
Within the clearance zone the asset owner sets, dig by hand or vacuum only, and support and protect exposed services as the owner requires.
Within the powerline no go zone, work only under the electricity entity's permit to work. Keep electrical leads off the metal frame with plastic lead hooks or insulation.
Work at floor level is broken up with breaks to stand and stretch.
Work at height is done from an EWP or from walkways with their guardrails fitted.
Work at height uses the plant's walkways and ladders once fitted with guardrails, or an elevating work platform, with harnesses where those are not yet in place.
Work at the pier head is done from an EWP, scaffold or under-bridge platform with guardrails.
Work from the floor or a platform. Where these cannot reach the work, ladders are used only after scaffolds and EWPs are considered.
Work from the floor with extendable tools, using access equipment only for glass these cannot reach. Where cleaning is near a balcony or open edge, the balustrade or barrier is in place first.
Work in hot weather follows the heat plan: shade, cool water, rest breaks and earlier start times.
Work is done from a platform ladder or mobile scaffold, not from a stepladder top.
Work is planned for the cooler part of the day in hot weather, with water and breaks.
Work on top of the stand is done from a platform ladder or scaffold, or with edge protection, not by climbing the stand.
Work stays inside the balustrades and barriers at tier fronts and vomitories, and no one climbs on them.

Workers are trained in using the scaffold. The scaffold stays level and plumb, castors are locked before anyone gets on, it is never moved with anyone on it, and it is accessed by its internal ladder.
Workers are trained to recognise buried contaminants and what action to take.
Workers using breakers or grinders (hand-arm vibration) with noise above 80 dB(A) LAeq,8h or 135 dB(C) peak have regular audiometric testing.
Working with arms overhead is a hazardous posture: rotate tasks and take short breaks.
